systemsMapSummary: Compliance is highest after patient contact (74%) and lowest before it (41%), which points away from knowledge and toward the moment itself. Three things pull compliance down at the before-contact moment. First, time pressure on the morning round: staff are 'three patients behind before you know it', so a detour to a dispenser competes with a full ward. Second, the environment sometimes fails at the point of care — a bed-bay dispenser is empty and there is no time to hunt for a refill, so the moment passes. Third, the social signal is mixed: when a senior clinician gels first, compliance rises; when they don't, juniors read stopping the round as awkward. These reinforce each other — a busy round, plus an empty dispenser, plus a senior who skipped, makes 'keep moving' the safest default. The highest-leverage moment is the before-contact step on the round, where gel must be literally within reach and the senior sets the tone.

topLeveragePoints.point: Put alcohol gel within arm's reach at every point of care and keep it filled
topLeveragePoints.currentState: 6 of 56 bed-bay dispensers were empty on spot check; staff say they 'don't have time to hunt for a refill'.

topLeveragePoints.point: Have the senior clinician gel first and visibly at the start of the round
topLeveragePoints.currentState: Compliance rises when a senior visibly gels first, but modelling is currently inconsistent.

topLeveragePoints.point: Add a brief before-contact cue to the morning-round routine
topLeveragePoints.currentState: Nothing on the busy round cues the before-contact moment, so it depends on memory under pressure.

headline: If gel were always within reach, seniors modelled it first on the round, and a simple cue marked the before-contact moment, we'd likely see Moment 1 compliance move from 41% toward the 90% target without more training.
